paragraphs: Mitya was fighting for breath as this wild speech burst out of him. He had turned white, his lips shook, and tears ran down his face.

“Yes, life is full. There’s life even underground,” he started again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but how I want to live now! Inside these peeling walls a hunger for existence and awareness has come over me. Rakitin can’t grasp that. All he wants is to build a house and rent out apartments. But you, I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering anyway? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no end to it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer a single question at the trial.... And I feel such strength in me now that I could bear anything, any pain at all, as long as I can say it to myself every moment: ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Stretched on the rack—I exist! Alone on top of a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I can’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And a whole life lies in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”
“What about Ivan?” Alyosha broke in, but Mitya didn’t hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before. They were buried in me. Maybe it was exactly because ideas I couldn’t understand were boiling up inside me that I drank and brawled and raged. I wanted to choke them down, quiet them, smother them. Ivan isn’t Rakitin. There’s an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx, and he says nothing. He’s always silent. It’s God who worries me. Nothing else worries me but that. What if He doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin is right and God is only an idea men invented? Then, without Him, man is lord of the earth and of the whole universe. Magnificent! Only how is man going to be good without God? That’s the question. I keep coming back to it. Who will man love, then? Who will he thank? Who will he sing the hymn to? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says you can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot could say so. I can’t make sense of it. Life’s easy for Rakitin. ‘Better think about extending civil rights, or about holding down the price of meat. That’s a simpler, more direct way to show your love for humanity than philosophy.’ And I told him, ‘Well, you without a God are the very man who’d raise the price of meat, if it suited you, and squeeze a rouble out of every kopeck.’ He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing to me and another to a Chinese man, so it’s relative. Or isn’t it? Isn’t it relative? A treacherous question! Don’t laugh when I tell you it’s kept me awake two nights. What amazes me now is that people can go on living and never give it a thought. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It’s beyond me. But he says nothing. I think he must be a Freemason. I asked him, and he said nothing. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul—and he was silent. Only once did he let a word slip.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha asked at once.

“I said to him, ‘So everything is lawful, if that’s the case?’ He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,’ he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were sound enough.’ That’s what slipped out of him, and that’s all he said. That beats Rakitin by a mile.”
“Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he here?”

“Later, I’ll tell you that later. Now I have to talk about something else. I haven’t told you anything about Ivan till now. I kept it for last. When all this is over here and the verdict is in, then I’ll tell you something. I’ll tell you everything. There’s something tremendous between us.... And you will be my judge in it. But don’t start on that now. Keep quiet. You talk about tomorrow, about the trial, but would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”
“Have you spoken with your lawyer?”

“What good is a lawyer? I told him the whole story. He’s a soft, city-bred rogue—a Bernard! And he doesn’t believe me, not a bit. Imagine, he thinks I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,’ I asked him, ‘why did you come to defend me?’ Hang the lot of them! They’ve even brought in a doctor to prove I’m mad. I won’t stand for that! And Katerina Ivanovna means to do her ‘duty’ to the end, whatever it costs her!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “That cat! That hard-hearted creature! She knows I said at Mokroe that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.’ It was repeated to her. Yes, the facts against me now are as many as the sands of the sea. Grigory holds to his story. Grigory is honest, but a fool. Plenty of people are honest because they’re fools. That’s Rakitin’s notion. Grigory is my enemy. And some people are worth more as enemies than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I’m afraid, oh, I’m afraid she’ll tell about how she bowed down to the ground over that four thousand. She’ll pay it back to the last farthing. I don’t want her sacrifice. They’ll shame me at the trial. I wonder how I’ll bear it. Go to her, Alyosha, and ask her not to bring that up in court. Can you do that? But the devil take it, it doesn’t matter! I’ll get through somehow. I don’t pity her. She’s done it to herself. She’s earned what she gets. I’ll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why must she suffer like this?” he cried out suddenly, in tears. “Grusha is killing me. Just thinking of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me a little while ago....”
“She told me you hurt her badly today.”
“I know. Damn my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry. I kissed her when she left. But I didn’t ask her to forgive me.”
“Why didn’t you?” Alyosha cried.
All at once Mitya laughed, almost cheerfully.

“May God spare you, my dear boy, from ever asking pardon for some fault from a woman you love. Above all from a woman you love, however badly you were in the wrong. Because a woman—who the devil can make out a woman? I know a little about them, at least. But just try owning up to a woman that you’re at fault. Say, ‘I’m sorry, forgive me,’ and the reproaches come down like rain! She won’t simply and plainly forgive you, not for anything. She’ll grind you into the dust, haul out things that never happened, call up everything, forget nothing, add some of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best of them, the very best, do this. She’ll scrape together every last scrap and pile it on your head. They’d skin you alive, I tell you, every one of them, these angels we can’t live without! I say it plainly and openly, dear boy: every decent man ought to be under some woman’s thumb. That’s my conviction—no, not conviction, my feeling. A man should be magnanimous, and there’s no disgrace in it for him! No disgrace for a hero, not even for a Cæsar! But all the same, never beg her pardon for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who’s been ruined by women. No, I’d better make it up to Grusha some other way, without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, I worship her. Only she doesn’t see it. No, she still thinks I don’t love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! Back then it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me. But now I’ve taken her whole soul into mine, and through her I’ve become a man myself. Will they let us marry? If they don’t, I’ll die of jealousy. Every day I imagine something.... What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha told him everything Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him go over certain things again, and seemed pleased.

“So she isn’t angry that I’m jealous?” he cried. “There’s a woman for you! ‘I’ve a fierce heart myself!’ Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can’t stand anyone being jealous of me. I can’t take it. We’ll fight. But I’ll love her, I’ll love her without end. Will they let us marry? Do they let convicts marry? That’s the question. And I can’t exist without her....”
Mitya crossed the room with a frown. It was nearly dark. All at once he seemed terribly uneasy.

“So there’s a secret, she says, a secret? We’ve hatched a plot against her, and Katya’s in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that’s not it. You’re far off the mark, with your silly woman’s ideas. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I’ll tell you our secret!”

He glanced around, stepped quickly up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered with an air of mystery, though in truth no one could hear them. The old warder was dozing in his corner, and not a word could reach the soldiers on guard.

“I’ll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered in a rush. “I meant to tell you later. How could I decide anything without you? You’re everything to me. I say Ivan is above us, but you are my angel. Your decision will be the one that settles it. Maybe it’s you who are above us and not Ivan. You see, it’s a matter of conscience, of the higher conscience—the secret is so important I can’t settle it myself, and I’ve held it back until I could talk to you. Still, it’s too early to decide now, since we have to wait for the verdict. The moment the verdict comes, you’ll decide my fate. Don’t decide now. I’ll tell you now. You listen, but don’t decide. Stand there and keep still. I won’t tell you all of it. I’ll just give you the idea, no details, and you keep still. No questions, no moving. Agreed? But good heavens, what am I going to do about your eyes? I’m afraid your eyes will tell me your decision even if you say nothing. Oh! I’m afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan proposes that I _escape_. I won’t give you the details. It’s all been thought through, it can all be arranged. Hush, don’t decide. I’d go to America with Grusha. You know I can’t live without Grusha! What if they won’t let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha, what would I do down there underground with a hammer? I’d only smash my own skull with the hammer! But then, on the other side, there’s my conscience. I’d have run away from suffering. A sign has come, and I’m refusing the sign. There’s a way of salvation open to me, and I’m turning my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the good will,’ I could do more good than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What is America? America is vanity again! And I expect there’s plenty of swindling in America too. I’d have run away from crucifixion! I’m telling you, Alexey, because you’re the only one who can understand this. There’s no one else. To everyone else it’s folly, madness, everything I’ve told you about the hymn. They’ll say I’ve lost my mind or I’m a fool. I haven’t lost my mind and I’m not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he won’t answer—he won’t speak. He doesn’t believe in the hymn. Don’t speak, don’t speak. I can see how you look! You’ve decided already. Don’t decide, spare me! I can’t live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”
Mitya finished, beside himself. He gripped Alyosha’s shoulders with both hands, and his feverish, yearning eyes were fixed on his brother’s.
“They don’t let convicts marry, do they?” he asked a third time, in a begging voice.
Alyosha had listened in great astonishment, and he was deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very set on this, and whose idea was it?”

“His, his, and he’s very set on it. At first he didn’t come to see me. Then suddenly he turned up a week ago and started in on it right away. He’s dead set on it. He doesn’t ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I’ll obey him, though I opened my whole heart to him as I have to you, and told him about the hymn too. He told me he’d arrange it. He’s found out everything. But more of that later. He’s just fixed on it. It all comes down to money: he’ll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says a magnificent escape can be arranged for ten thousand.”
“And he told you not to tell me, on any account?” Alyosha asked again.

“Not to tell anyone, and above all not you. Not to tell you on any account. No doubt he’s afraid you’ll stand in front of me as my conscience. Don’t tell him I told you. Don’t tell him, whatever happens.”
“You’re right,” said Alyosha. “It’s impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you’ll decide for yourself. Then you’ll find that new man in you, and he will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who’ll decide _à la_ Bernard, because I think I’m a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.
“But brother, do you have no hope at all of being acquitted?”

Mitya shrugged nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it’s time you went,” he said, suddenly hurrying. “I hear the superintendent shouting in the yard. He’ll be in here any minute. We’re late, it’s against the rules. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Make the sign of the cross over me, darling, for the cross I have to carry tomorrow.”
They embraced and kissed.
“Ivan,” Mitya said suddenly, “proposes that I escape. But of course he believes I did it.”
A sorrowful smile crossed his lips.
“Did you ask him whether he believes it?” asked Alyosha.
“No, I didn’t. I wanted to, but I couldn’t. I hadn’t the nerve. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-by!”
They kissed again in a hurry, and Alyosha was already on his way out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

“Stand facing me! There, like that!” And once more he grabbed Alyosha, with both hands on his shoulders. His face went white all at once, so white that it showed dreadfully even in the failing light. His lips twitched, and his eyes bored into Alyosha.
“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as if you stood before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you yourself, believe it? The whole truth, don’t lie!” he cried in desperation.
Everything seemed to heave and sway before Alyosha, and he felt something like a knife go into his heart.
“Hush! What are you saying?” he stammered helplessly.
“The whole truth, all of it, don’t lie!” Mitya repeated.
“Not for one moment have I believed you were the murderer!” The words came in a shaking voice from deep in Alyosha’s chest, and he raised his right hand into the air as though calling God to witness.
Mitya’s whole face shone with joy.

“Thank you!” he said slowly, like a man breathing out after a faint. “You’ve given me new life now. Would you believe it, until this moment I was afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well, go! You’ve given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Come on, go! Love Ivan!” Those were Mitya’s last words.

Alyosha left in tears. Mitya’s mistrust, his lack of faith even in him, in Alyosha—all of it suddenly opened up to Alyosha a depth of hopeless grief and despair in his unhappy brother’s soul that he had never suspected. Intense, endless pity swept over him at once. His torn heart ached sharply. “Love Ivan!”—he suddenly remembered Mitya’s words. And he was on his way to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He worried about Ivan as much as about Mitya, and now more than ever.
